text: This is Lamplighter. It's an AI agent that wins back revenue for Razorpay merchants, and it's rendered as a cozy town. Built for the Razorpay AI Buildathon, track three, by Nipun Arora.

Meet Saanjh and Co., a small tea and candle studio in Jaipur. Every week, money quietly slips away. A UPI request times out. A card hits its daily limit. A bank goes down for ten minutes. An autopay mandate gets paused. A wholesale invoice drifts past due. Every one of these is recoverable. But chasing them by hand is slow, and a dumb cron job just annoys customers and breaks the rules.
So here's the idea. Every customer is a house. Every payment at risk is a dark lantern. And the agent is a lamplighter, walking the streets, relighting them, inside the rules.

Press light the lamps, and it begins. Every case gets diagnosed first. Razorpay's structured error handles the easy ones. For the messy ones, a local Qwen model, running right here on this laptop, reads the raw bank string, something like U30, debit has been failed, and works out what actually went wrong. Then the policy engine lays out every possible action, and runs every rule against it. The model only ever picks from what's already allowed. And every message it sends creates a real Razorpay test mode order.

Click any house, and you can see the whole story. The Razorpay error, with the raw bank response. The diagnosis, its confidence, and whether the rules or the model made that call. Then every action the agent considered, with the exact rules that blocked it. A silent retry is off the table when the issuer says don't retry. A voice call is blocked when the amount is too small to justify one. And the message goes out in the customer's own language, Hinglish or English, checked for the right amount, the merchant name, and an opt out line.

And here's the loop actually closing. The customer opens the pay page, and pays through Razorpay checkout. The server verifies the signature, captures the payment, and the lantern lights up. If the browser never calls back, polling catches it anyway.

Now watch what happens at nine at night. The lamplighter stops. Quiet hours aren't a footnote here, they're part of the world. Anything deferred shows up in the journal, ready for nine in the morning. And if a customer replies stop, that's it. Contact ends immediately, including any retry that was already scheduled. Three knocks maximum. No repeats. Do not disturb respected. And every extra knock costs goodwill in the maths.

So, the numbers. Across a hundred and twenty cases, over a simulated fortnight, Lamplighter recovered three lakh forty one thousand rupees, out of ten point seven lakh at risk. The naive retry cron, on exactly the same customers, got one lakh thirty six thousand. Fifty nine cases against nineteen. Half the touches. Eleven complaints against fifty five. And zero policy violations, against three hundred and fifty eight. Diagnosis accuracy went from seventy two percent on rules alone, to a hundred percent once the local model reads the bank strings. Run it across ten different seeded worlds, and the agent wins all ten, on money and on complaints, with a confidence interval that excludes zero. And to be clear, these customers are simulated, with hidden state the agent never sees. The report says so plainly.

Failure here is exercised, not just promised. Chaos injection makes Razorpay and the model fail on demand. There are retries with backoff, a circuit breaker the engine waits out, and template fallbacks when the model writes something that breaks a rule. Every step lands in a hash chained audit log that anyone can verify. Twenty five tests, and continuous integration that runs a whole batch with no external services at all.
Escalations go to a human, with a packet of everything that was tried. That's Lamplighter. Bounded, explainable, and measured. Thank you.
